Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A small red sailboat with a white sail on a calm turquoise sea at sunset, with the low sun, its golden path on the water, and a purple mountain on the far shore.

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

10 stepsCanvas: 14 x 11 inFocal point: The sailboat, right of center (69% across, 45% down in the frame), with the sun and its golden path as a second point of interest left of center. Light: The setting sun, low in the sky left of the boat (41% across, 42% down in the frame), lighting the sky and water from behind; the sail's lit side faces the sun.How this lesson was made

What you need

Tubes

  • Titanium white
  • Cadmium yellow medium (hue)
  • Cadmium red medium (hue)
  • Ultramarine blue
  • Burnt sienna

Brushes

  • 1 inch flat: covering and blending the whole skyFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #8 round: dabbing the sun discRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 1/2 inch flat: the mountain's edge and fill, and the shoreline stripFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #6 round: outlining and filling the hullRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • Liner (#1): the mast and boomLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass
  • #4 round: the sparkle dashesRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press

Also

  • A 14 x 11 in canvas, landscape (hang it that way). Positions in the steps are percentages across and down: each 10% is 1.4 in across and 1.1 in down.
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

Your paints

Every paint in the lesson. You don't have to mix them all at the start: each step lists the paints it uses with their recipes, so you can mix a little as you go before it dries. Parts are by volume.

The steps

Step 1Step 2Step 3Step 4Step 5Step 6Step 7Step 8Step 9Step 10

STEP 1 OF 10

Blend the sunset sky

  1. The light comes from the setting sun, low and a little left of center; every highlight faces left.
  2. With the 1 inch flat and creamy Twilight violet, long side-to-side strokes across the top 10%.
  3. Sunset pink to 22% down, Sunset orange to 45%, then orange with a little pink down to a straight edge at 62% (6.8 in). X-stroke each join while wet.
  4. X-stroke Glow gold in a soft patch 39% across, 40% down. Done: a smooth gradient, white below 62%.
Paints for this step4 paints, 4 new
  • Twilight violet new1 part ultramarine, 1 part white, a touch of red
  • Sunset pink new3 parts white, 2 parts red, 1 part ultramarine
  • Sunset orange new2 parts red, 1 part yellow, 1 part white
  • Glow gold new3 parts yellow, 2 parts red, 2 parts white

Colors dry a little darker: test each mix on the palette edge first.

Mix plenty of Sunset orange: it covers the biggest area and you'll use it again for the sun path.

Brushes

1 inch flat

Strokes

Long horizontal blend. Pull the flat edge to edge across the canvas in level strokes, overlapping each one a little.

X stroke. Criss-cross over each join between colors in small X shapes so they melt together.

Watch out: Run the orange below the horizon line (54%) to 62% down; the mountain and water go over it.

Watch out: Stop blending once the paint drags. Streaks are fine.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

No diagram: A gradient: the picture and the band positions are enough.

STEP 2 OF 10

Paint the sun

  1. Let the sky dry.
  2. With the #8 round and creamy Sun cream, dab a circle about 0.8 in wide, centered 39% across and 42.5% down, working from the center out.
  3. Let it dry and add a second coat so no orange shows through. Done: a clean, bright round sun.
Paints for this step1 paint, 1 new
  • Sun cream new2 parts white, 1 part yellow, a touch of red

Brushes

#8 round

Strokes

Dabbing. Touch the round's tip down in small overlapping dabs, spiraling out from the center to a clean round edge.

Watch out: Light over orange needs 2 coats; wait between them.

Watch out: Trace a coin or bottle cap lightly in pencil first if a freehand circle is hard.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 3 OF 10

Paint the mountain and the far shore

  1. Let the sky dry. Mark the horizon with a ruler: a light pencil line 54% down (5.9 in).
  2. With the 1/2 inch flat and creamy Mountain purple, pull the mountain's top edge: from the left edge 40% down, over a low peak near the edge, sloping down to 40% across. Fill below with side-to-side strokes.
  3. Lay the values in the table on the mountain while wet.
  4. With Shore navy and the flat's edge, pull a straight strip across the whole width, from 50% down to the pencil line. Done: orange sky still shows from 54% to 62%.
Build the depth, dark first

Brushes

1/2 inch flat

Strokes

Horizontal strokes for flat ground. Keep the flat level and pull long strokes; use its chisel edge for the strip's straight top and bottom.

Watch out: Keep the strip level; a tilted horizon makes the sea look like it's draining.

STEP 4 OF 10

Lay in the water

  1. With the 1 inch flat and creamy Turquoise water, paint long level strokes from the navy strip down to about 70% down.
  2. Paint Deep teal from the bottom edge up, and blend it into the turquoise while wet with long horizontal strokes.
  3. Done: water covers everything below the strip, no white canvas anywhere.

Brushes

1 inch flat

Strokes

Long horizontal blend. Edge-to-edge level strokes; go back over the turquoise-teal join while both are wet.

Watch out: Keep every stroke level.

Watch out: It may look flat and plain right now. That's the ugly stage, and it's normal.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 5 OF 10

Add ripples to the water

  1. Let the water dry.
  2. With the 1/2 inch flat and nearly dry Deep teal, make short horizontal dashes across the water: small and close near the horizon, longer (up to 1.5 in) toward the bottom.
  3. Then add Turquoise water dashes with a little white between them. Done: the base still shows between the dashes.

Brushes

1/2 inch flat

Strokes

Dry brush dashes. Wipe most paint off, then touch and pull the flat sideways in short level dashes.

Watch out: Don't cover the base completely; ripples are broken marks.

Watch out: Try a few dashes on scrap paper first.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 6 OF 10

Paint the sun's path on the water

  1. Let the ripples dry.
  2. With the 1/2 inch flat and creamy Sunset orange, make short horizontal dashes in a column under the sun, shaped as in the diagram: 34% to 47% across at the horizon, widest (15% to 55%) at 70-80% down, narrowing below.
  3. Add Glow gold dashes over the middle of the column, and a few stray orange dashes out on the left water. Done: teal shows between the dashes.

Brushes

1/2 inch flat

Strokes

Horizontal dashes. Touch the flat down and pull it sideways about an inch, then lift. Shorter dashes near the horizon.

Watch out: Leave gaps between the dashes; a solid stripe looks like a road, not light on water.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 7 OF 10

Paint the red hull

  1. Let the water dry.
  2. Build the hull as in the diagram: about 2.9 in long, from 63% to 84% across. Its pointed left end rises to 57% down; the top edge slopes to about 60% at the blunt right end.
  3. Outline it with the #6 round and creamy Boat red, then fill it in.
  4. Let it dry and add a second coat. Done: a solid red hull on the water.

Brushes

#6 round

Strokes

Building from pieces. Pull the sloped top line first, from the raised point on the left, then the curved bottom, then fill between.

Watch out: Keep the waterline along the bottom level with the horizon; only the top edge slopes.

Heads up, this picture is a little off: The plan's looks_like put the hull's pointed bow on the right, but the finish and the step picture have the raised point on the left with the top edge sloping down to the right. Spotted through the step review. Paint what the steps say.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 8 OF 10

Paint the sails and the mast

  1. Let the hull dry.
  2. Build the sails as in the diagram: the mast's line rises from the hull at 72% across to 26% down (about 3.4 in tall).
  3. With the #6 round and creamy Sail white, fill the left triangle (lower corner 64% across) and the right one (down to 57% down, out to 81% across). Two coats.
  4. While wet, lay the values in the table.
  5. Let it dry. With the liner and inky Mast brown, pull the mast, then the boom along the right sail's bottom edge.

STEP 9 OF 10

Paint the boat's reflection

  1. Let the water dry.
  2. With the 1/2 inch flat and creamy Boat red, make short horizontal dashes just under the hull, from 63% to 67% down, as wide as the hull.

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: A red sailboat on a turquoise sea at sunset, with the sun, its path on the water, and a purple mountain.

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: No bars, borders, captions, or surroundings.

Fitted to your canvas

Canvas: 14 x 11 in, landscape (an 11x14 hung sideways, following the 3:2 landscape picture)

Done: crop

Left out: the left 15%: the foot of the mountain and some open water

Why: Cropping the 3:2 picture to the canvas's 14:11 shape loses 15% and keeps the boat, its reflection, the sun, and its path whole. The focal point (the boat, 76% across) pushes the crop to the right edge, so all of the loss is on the left.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: No tiny separate things (the boat is the subject), no textures of hundreds of items (the water is one repeated dash), no detail inside big shapes, and about 8 parts, within the budget of 8 for an 11x14 (154 sq in, so max_parts as is).

Changed: none

Why: Already beginner-sized.

A calm sunset seascape that is already painterly: a smooth violet-to-orange sky, a low cream sun with a golden path on the water, a purple mountain on the far shore, and a small red sailboat with a white sail and a broken reflection. Nothing is busy. What's hard for a beginner is the smooth sky blend, keeping the horizon level, and keeping the reflections broken instead of solid. The lesson is about a clean gradient sky and water made of horizontal dashes.

Subject: A small red sailboat with a white sail on a calm turquoise sea at sunset, with the low sun, its golden path on the water, and a purple mountain on the far shore.
Focal point: The sailboat, right of center (69% across, 45% down in the frame), with the sun and its golden path as a second point of interest left of center.
Light: The setting sun, low in the sky left of the boat (41% across, 42% down in the frame), lighting the sky and water from behind; the sail's lit side faces the sun.

What it saw, back to front

  1. sky gradient (violet, pink, orange, gold glow)
  2. sun
  3. far mountain and shoreline strip
  4. water base gradient
  5. water ripples
  6. sun path on the water
  7. boat hull
  8. sails, mast, and boom
  9. boat reflection
  10. highlights
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front

The owner named it (acrylic-paint-along-beginner).

ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

A simple back-to-front scene: sky, sun, far shore, water, then the boat in front. That is exactly the paint-along order.

Passed onBlock in, then build up (acrylic-block-in-beginner)

A toned ground and sketch add steps a scene this simple doesn't need, and the owner named paint-along.

How the paint recipes were worked out13 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

    Written by eye first: 3 parts white, 2 parts red, a touch of ultramarine blue

Why the steps go in this order10 steps

Back to front: the sky first, run below the horizon so its strokes stay long; the sun on the dry sky; the far mountain and shore strip; the water over the sky's lower edge; ripples, then the sun path as separate texture passes; then the boat from the hull up, its reflection, and the brightest highlights last.

  1. 1. Blend the sunset sky

    Farthest back and the biggest area; a wet blend done in one go.

  2. 2. Paint the sun

    Sits in the sky, behind everything else, and needs a dry sky under it to stay clean.

  3. 3. Paint the mountain and the far shore

    The next layer forward; it sets the horizon line everything else lines up with.

  4. 4. Lay in the water

    Covers the rest of the canvas and the sky's overrun below the horizon.

  5. 5. Add ripples to the water

    Texture split from the base so no step jumps from flat to textured.

  6. 6. Paint the sun's path on the water

    Light on the water goes over the ripples and under the boat.

  7. 7. Paint the red hull

    The subject's biggest piece first.

  8. 8. Paint the sails and the mast

    Painted over the hull's top edge and the sky behind; values from one white base.

  9. 9. Paint the boat's reflection

    Needs the boat finished to copy its colors.

  10. 10. Add the brightest highlights

    Brightest touches last, as the technique asks.

Where Claude drew diagrams3 steps, free

Two steps add shaped objects whole (the hull, then the sails and mast), and one step's dash column has a shape the words couldn't carry (the sun path), so those three get diagrams; everything else is a gradient, a flat shape, or one repeated dash.

  • Step 6: Paint the sun's path on the water step review proposal, 2026-11-11

    Noticed: The step review found the text said the column widens to the bottom, while the picture is widest at 70-80% down and narrows below. The column's outline is a shape, so show it.

    Pieces: The column's outline over the horizon and sun (already painted), then level dashes inside it, longer lower down, gold in the middle.

  • Step 7: Paint the red hull beginner check, corrected from the step review

    Noticed: The hull appears whole in one step, and its shape (a raised point on the left, a sloped top, a shallow curved bottom) is hard to get from a 3 in red sliver. The step review caught that my first text said to keep the top level, which the picture doesn't show.

    Pieces: The sloped top line first, from the raised left point, because it sets the boat's direction; then one shallow curve underneath to the blunt right end.

  • Step 8: Paint the sails and the mast beginner check

    Noticed: Two triangles and two lines whose placement depends on the mast; easy to get the triangles leaning wrong.

    Pieces: The mast as one vertical line, then the tall narrow left triangle against it, then the wider right one with the boom along its base.

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • fit-canvas (tool): when the photo already has the model frame's shape (3:2 here) and the mode is crop, the bands outside the canvas are exactly the part the crop cut off. The frame could be the original photo with the canvas box placed over the crop, with no band-fill render. Here the render came from the cache, but a first run would pay about $0.04 at medium for content the photo already has.
  • fit-canvas (tool): the focal point pushes the crop all the way to one side when the subject sits off center (boat at 76%), so all the loss came off the left and cut into the mountain. Centering the crop (loss split 7.5% each side) would also have kept the boat whole and more of the mountain; the tool has no way to prefer the plainest edges.
  • grid --cells 10 draws squares, so on a 14:11 canvas crop the rows are 12.7% tall and on the 3:2 frame 15%, not 10%. The skill says to measure 10% steps on it; I measured in pixels instead. A grid with 10 rows and 10 columns would match the page's 'each 10% is 1.4 in across and 1.1 in down'.
  • The first sky render stopped at 55% down instead of the planned 62%, the same failure the balloon rerun saw. A pixel count in the prompt fix ('about 635 pixels from the top of 1024') worked on the redo.
  • Deep teal is out of reach of the five tubes (Delta E 9.8): without a phthalo or cerulean, a bright cyan-teal sea goes grayer. The research doesn't cover which tube a beginner should add for tropical water.
  • The plan said the hull's pointed bow was on the right; the finish and every render put the raised point on the left. I read the boat from the grid image too quickly. The step review caught it through the step text; check a subject's direction (bow, head, face) on the canvas crop before writing looks_like.
  • Step review drift: most renders repaint a little of what was finished before (sun-path ripples, the sun path again in the hull and reflection steps, the hull trim appearing in the sails step, a brighter reflection in the finish). Parallel renders from the finish have no way to hold earlier steps fixed; compositing (#8) would.
  • stroke_results has no entry for short broken horizontal dashes on water, the most-used mark in this lesson (sun path, reflection, ripples, sparkles); the research should add one.
